films.title: Princess Mononoke
films.description: People and forces of nature clash as a visitor tries to understand whether survival must always create enemies.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: No inherited or imperial title is treated as legitimate; the Mikado's charter to 'subdue the Deer God' is shown as greed-driven and Asano's samurai as predatory. Legitimacy is located instead in the continuation of life itself and in reciprocal coexistence — authority earned by caring for dependents (Eboshi over Irontown, Moro over her tribe) and validated by the choice to keep living rather than to dominate.
skeleton.opening_power: Dispersed and contested: Lady Eboshi holds Irontown and its firearms; the animal gods (Moro, Okkoto, Nago) hold the forest; the distant Emperor and Lord Asano press claims from outside; Ashitaka's Emishi are a remnant driven east five centuries ago.
skeleton.closing_power: Still dispersed but chastened: Eboshi, one-armed, retains leadership of a burned Irontown pledging to 'start over again'; San holds the regrown but changed forest; the great animal gods and the Forest Spirit are dead; Jigo and the Emperor's expedition have failed and withdrawn.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Biological life — the devastated land is renewed with flora, Ashitaka's curse is lifted, and Irontown's community survives to rebuild.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: The age of the great forest gods ends permanently: the Forest Spirit, Moro, Okkoto and Nago are dead, the old-growth woods are felled, and San concedes 'even if they grow back, they won't be the Deer God's woods.' The imperial errand for immortality is exposed as folly.
skeleton.antagonist: No single antagonist; the nearest are Lady Eboshi as belligerent and Jigo as the Emperor's cynical agent
skeleton.antagonist_origin: Eboshi shot Nago and clears the forest in order to sustain a settlement she built as a refuge for brothel girls she bought free and lepers she personally nursed — 'She is the only one who looked upon us as human.'
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: The hatred and rage carried in his cursed arm — the temptation to answer violence with violence and to take one side of the war.
skeleton.protagonist_change: He refuses to join either side ('All that does is cause more hatred'), insists on seeing 'with eyes unclouded,' and PUTS DOWN the curse — the imposed hatred is lifted from him. He also puts down his inherited role as the Emishi's future leader, choosing to stay at the ironworks rather than take up any throne.
skeleton.final_image: Regrown green land and a surviving kodama in the renewed forest, with Ashitaka and San parted but pledged to meet — Irontown to be rebuilt, the old gods gone.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: I give up... You can't win against fools!
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The film is sincere about its conflict rather than ironic: reception describes it as 'not a simplistic tale of good and evil' and notes the ending is 'ambiguous' — 'the Forest Spirit's death revives nature, but the wild forests remain felled.' It criticizes environmental destruction while 'grudgingly [admitting]' some conflict is inevitable, and it validates Ashitaka's mediating position through the dialogue it rewards ('Together we'll live'). It does subvert jidaigeki convention by denying the Emperor and samurai sanctity, but it endorses the coexistence it depicts rather than critiquing it.
skeleton.source_text: Original screenplay by Hayao Miyazaki; conceptually inspired by the Epic of Gilgamesh and influenced by Sasuke Nakao's evergreen forest culture theory
skeleton.inverts_source_how: Subverts jidaigeki convention by refusing 'the portrayals of the Emperor and the samurai as sacred and noble,' and by placing women, former prostitutes and people with leprosy at the center of industry and arms-making; also refuses the deus ex machina resolution of the Nausicaa film adaptation.

films.title: Starship Troopers
films.description: Young citizens join a vast military project and slowly confront the stories a society tells about duty and enemies.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Force. The order the film depicts locates legitimate authority in violence and in citizenship earned by federal service — 'force, my friends, is violence, the supreme authority from which all other authority is derived' — with the veterans' seizure of power after 'the failure of democracy' treated in-world as the founding legitimate act. The telling, however, frames this legitimacy claim as propaganda rather than truth.
skeleton.opening_power: The United Citizen Federation — a stratocracy founded by 'veterans' who 'took control and imposed the stability that has lasted for generations'; power sits with Sky Marshals, the Federal Council, officers, and the FedNet propaganda apparatus. Civilians (Rico's parents) have wealth but no political standing.
skeleton.closing_power: The same United Citizen Federation, undiminished and re-legitimised: Sky Marshal and Federal command intact, Carl a colonel who admits sending troops knowingly to die, Carmen a captain, Rico a lieutenant. The surviving protagonists now staff the apparatus and appear inside its recruitment broadcast.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Confidence in the war machine after the Klendathu catastrophe. The humiliation of defeat and the revelation that command treats its own troops as expendable are absorbed and forgotten; morale, the recruitment cycle and the promise of victory are put back exactly as they were in the opening advertisement, which the final scene reprises almost shot for shot.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Nothing in the order. What is dismantled is private life: Rico's family, home city, civilian future, and both women he loves. The captured Brain Bug ends the Arachnids' strategic invisibility, but no political arrangement changes and 'no actual conclusion is offered.'
skeleton.antagonist: The Arachnids, personified late by the Brain Bug — though the telling positions the Federation itself as the object of critique.
skeleton.antagonist_origin: The film plants, and then visually discredits, the suggestion that humans provoked the war by colonising Arachnid worlds and that the bugs are defending themselves — the journalist who asks whether 'a live and let live policy is preferable' is torn apart on camera mid-sentence.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Rico enlists for private reasons — 'I joined up for her. I wouldn't even be here if it wasn't for her' — and is driven by personal wanting-to-win ('I wanted to win, sir!'), which gets a squadmate killed and nearly makes him quit.
skeleton.protagonist_change: He TAKES UP what is handed to him: the corporal's, then sergeant's, then lieutenant's rank, and finally Rasczak's own words verbatim ('Everyone fights. No one quits'). He puts down nothing imposed on him; he surrenders private attachment and becomes the ideal instrument of the state, articulating its catechism ('A citizen has the courage to make the safety of the human race their personal responsibility') that he could not believe in the opening classroom.
skeleton.final_image: A FedNet recruitment broadcast: the Brain Bug under vivisection, then Captain Carmen Ibanez ordering a drop and Lieutenant Rico charging his troops forward with Rasczak's line, over the caption-slogan of the film's own first scene. It asserts that the cycle is beginning again with the survivors now cast as the bait.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: Service guarantees citizenship.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The themes and reception layers settle it: Verhoeven 'used Starship Troopers to deconstruct and undermine these themes' and said 'whenever you see something that you think is fascist, you should know that the filmmakers agree with your opinion'; Nazi/Fascist iconography is used for the sympathetic side; the FedNet segments ('children... stamping on cockroaches while an adult looks on happily') are described as satire; the ending is read as the survivors 'not disagreeing with this system or choosing to fight against it, but becoming a part of it by appearing in recruitment propaganda.' Countervailing evidence exists and is recorded: many 1997 critics read the fascism as sincere, and the Rotten Tomatoes consensus is merely 'A fun movie.'
skeleton.source_text: Robert A. Heinlein's novel Starship Troopers
skeleton.inverts_source_how: Verhoeven read the novel as 'fascistic, nationalistic, totalitarian, and in favor of military rule' and reversed its valence, keeping the plot and rhetoric while framing them as propaganda; Rico, revealed as Filipino at the end of the novel, is made white 'to further satirize the fascistic messaging.'

films.title: Fight Club
films.description: A dissatisfied man finds belonging in a secret movement that promises freedom while demanding a new kind of obedience.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Self-determination grounded in personal responsibility: the film locates legitimate authority neither in the corporate-consumer order (depicted as fraudulent and lethal — the recall formula, 'slaves with white collars') nor in Tyler's charismatic revolutionary command (depicted as fascistic, 'You are not special... maggots'), but in the individual who owns his own acts — 'I am responsible for all of it, and I accept that.'
skeleton.opening_power: The corporate-consumer order: an unnamed automobile company that prices deaths by formula, credit-card institutions, advertising and IKEA catalogue identity; over the Narrator personally, Tyler Durden holds power — the film opens with Tyler's gun in the Narrator's mouth, three minutes from a demolition the Narrator did not choose.
skeleton.closing_power: The Narrator holds power over himself, having 'killed' Tyler; but Project Mayhem's apparatus survives intact and executes its plan — the space monkeys still call him 'Mr. Durden,' still take orders, and the credit-company towers come down on schedule. Institutional power over debt records is destroyed and nothing is installed in its place.
skeleton.what_is_restored: The Narrator's singular selfhood and his capacity for connection with Marla — the intimacy he had avoided is finally taken up ('I really like you, Marla'). Nothing of the prior social order is restored.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: The consumer-credit debt record and the buildings housing it; the Narrator's identity as a possession-defined 'by-product of a lifestyle obsession'; Tyler Durden as an autonomous authority inside him.
skeleton.antagonist: Tyler Durden — who is revealed to be the Narrator's own projection
skeleton.antagonist_origin: Tyler is invented by an insomniac, fatherless, consumer-numbed 'thirty-year-old boy' who 'was looking for a way to change your life' and 'could not do this on your own' — a wish-figure grown out of paternal abandonment ('If our fathers bailed, what does that tell you about God?') and generational purposelessness.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Passivity and self-anaesthesia: he defines himself by purchases, cannot ask for what he needs ('Three pitchers of beer and you still can't ask'), borrows other people's dying to feel anything, avoids intimacy with Marla, and disclaims responsibility for the deaths his job files as statistics.
skeleton.protagonist_change: He PUTS DOWN the imposed persona and the ideology handed to him — refusing Tyler's authority, shooting himself to be rid of it — and in the same movement takes up ownership of what he did ('I am responsible for all of it, and I accept that') and takes Marla's hand. The film ends with a renunciation, not an inheritance.
skeleton.final_image: The Narrator, shot through the face, stands holding Marla's hand at a window as the credit-company skyscrapers collapse in sequence. The image asserts that the self has been reunified and a human connection made, while the destruction he set in motion proceeds without him and without any proposed replacement.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: You met me at a very strange time in my life.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The analysis states the film 'only half-accepts the revolutionary dialectic by Tyler Durden; the Narrator pulls back and rejects Durden's ideas,' that Tyler's 'methods become dehumanizing' and that he orders men about 'with a megaphone similar to camp directors at Chinese re-education camps.' Fincher: 'I love this idea that you can have fascism without offering any direction or solution... this movie couldn't be further from offering any kind of solution.' Reception confirms the ambiguity is contested rather than settled — Maslin warned it 'could be misconstrued as an endorsement of violence and nihilism,' Walker called it 'A Nazi piece of work,' while the film's makers called it 'an accurate portrayal of men in the 1990s.' The critique is real but the seduction is filmed with relish, hence the flag with reservations.
interiority_granted: The Narrator (continuous first-person voiceover, dreams, self-diagnoses — 'I am Jack's broken heart')
Tyler Durden (given full argumentative voice, though as an extension of the Narrator's interior)
interiority_withheld: Marla Singer (seen and heard, never narrated from inside; a critic notes the failure 'to make Bonham Carter's character interesting')
The rank-and-file space monkeys, deliberately depersonalised until death
punished: The Narrator (beaten, burned, shot through the cheek)
Bob (shot in the head serving Project Mayhem)
forgiven: The Narrator — survives, keeps Marla, is not arrested
Marla Singer — protected and finally accepted
Bob — restored a name in death: 'His name is Robert Paulsen'

The things you own end up owning you.
We're the middle children of history, men. No purpose or place.
His name is Robert Paulsen.

films.title: The Matrix
films.description: An ordinary worker is offered a terrifying explanation for the world and must choose comfort or a difficult awakening.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Self-determination and awakened knowledge of the truth — authority is legitimate when it frees minds to choose, illegitimate when it maintains comfortable illusion for the purpose of control. The film also treats prophecy/fate as a genuine warrant, but only once the chosen one affirms it by his own belief ('I can only show you the door. You have to walk through it.')
skeleton.opening_power: The machines and their sentient enforcement programs (the Agents), who run the Matrix and farm humanity for energy; within the simulation, corporate and police authority (Rhineheart, the police, the Agents) hold sway over Thomas Anderson.
skeleton.closing_power: Still the machines in material terms — the Matrix remains standing, Zion survives — but Neo now holds unbounded power inside the system and addresses the machines as an equal who can rewrite it: 'I'm going to show them a world without you.'
skeleton.what_is_restored: Morpheus is rescued and his faith vindicated; the crew of the Nebuchadnezzar survives the Sentinel attack; the prophecy of the One is confirmed rather than revised.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Neo's status as an ordinary, obedient employee and the Matrix's monopoly on reality — the system's rules no longer bind him, Agent Smith's supposed invincibility is broken, and the illusion is declared revocable.
skeleton.antagonist: Agent Smith, and behind him the machine order that built the Matrix; Cypher as the internal betrayer.
skeleton.antagonist_origin: Smith is a program bound to the Matrix who loathes his confinement among humans and wants Zion's destruction so he can be released ('I hate this place... I must get out of here. I must get free'), while Cypher's betrayal is explained by exhaustion and the misery of the real world ('I'm tired of this war... Ignorance is bliss').
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Disbelief — in fate, in the truth of his situation, and above all in himself; he insists 'I don't like the idea that I'm not in control of my life' and later 'I'm not the One... I'm just another guy.'
skeleton.protagonist_change: He TAKES UP the role handed to him — the mantle of the One conferred by Morpheus's faith, the Oracle's guidance and Trinity's love — replacing doubt with knowledge ('Don't think you are. Know you are'), and simultaneously PUTS DOWN the imposed identity of Thomas Anderson ('My name is Neo').
skeleton.final_image: Neo hangs up a payphone inside the Matrix after warning the system that he will show the sleeping population a world without rules, then flies upward out of the city — an assertion that the awakened individual can now break the order from within, and that the story just ends is only a beginning.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: Where we go from there is a choice I leave to you.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The ending rewards belief without irony: Morpheus's faith is vindicated ('I knew it. He's the One'), Trinity's declaration of love literally resurrects Neo, and the closing monologue is delivered straight as a liberation manifesto. Reception treats it as earnest rather than satirical — 'a pretty compelling call to the dead-above-the-eyeballs masses to unite and cast off their chains', and 'those who have suggested that the film explores significant philosophical and spiritual themes'; critics who dislike it call it 'pseudo-spiritual hokum', not irony.
interiority_granted: Cypher (his motive is voiced at length)
Agent Smith (his revulsion and desire for freedom are voiced)
interiority_withheld: the enslaved human population in the fields
forgiven: Neo (for his earlier disbelief and for surrendering to the Agents)
Morpheus (for the deception of freeing a mind past the safe age — 'I owe you an apology')
evidence_quotes: That you are a slave. Like everyone else, you were born into bondage
This is your last chance. After this, there is no turning back.
I'm trying to free your mind, Neo. But I can only show you the door. You have to walk through it.
Human beings are a disease. A cancer of this planet. You are a plague. And we are the cure.
If I had to choose between that and the Matrix I choose the Matrix.
Goodbye, Mr. Anderson. / My name is Neo.

films.title: Billy Elliot
films.description: A young person discovers a calling that challenges the role his family and community have prepared for him.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Self-determination and individual talent \u2014 the film locates legitimate authority in a person's right to express themselves, and in a family's freely given consent to that, rather than in inherited class role, paternal command or communal solidarity; Mrs Wilkinson's 'This is when you go out and find life' and the mother's letter 'Always be yourself' are the film's authorising texts, and the Royal Ballet School's institutional judgement is treated as fair.
skeleton.opening_power: Jackie the father, backed by Tony and the masculine order of the boxing hall and the striking union, holds authority over Billy; beyond them, an unseen state (Thatcher, the police) holds power over the community.
skeleton.closing_power: Billy holds authority over his own life \u2014 an adult professional dancer on a London stage, watched from the audience by his father, brother and Michael; the miners have lost and returned to work.
skeleton.what_is_restored: The father-son bond, and the family's ability to be proud of itself; Jackie is returned to the picket line and to solidarity with Tony after his attempt to scab is stopped.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: The gendered rule that boys box and girls dance; the assumption that a mining boy inherits the mine; the strike itself is broken and the industrial community's future dismantled; the taboo silence around Michael's homosexuality.
skeleton.antagonist: Jackie Elliot \u2014 the father's prohibition, which stands in for the community's policed masculinity and class fatalism; behind him, impersonally, the state and the collapse of the pits.
skeleton.antagonist_origin: A widowed miner ground down by poverty and a losing strike ('Look at the state of us, man. What we got to offer the poor sod?'), whose own mother-in-law was denied training and who fears his son will be despised as a 'poof' and a 'scab'.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Concealment and shame \u2014 Billy hides the dancing, cannot say what it is for, calls himself 'a right sissy' and lashes out (at Mrs Wilkinson, at the boy at the audition) when frustrated.
skeleton.protagonist_change: He acquires articulacy and unembarrassed self-possession \u2014 the audition speech ('Like there's fire in me body... Like electricity') is the film's turning point. He ends by TAKING UP something offered: the place at the school, the family's raised money, his father's blessing; and simultaneously by PUTTING DOWN the imposed inheritance of the pit and the boxing gloves.
skeleton.final_image: Billy, 25, leaps onto the stage as the Swan in Swan Lake while Jackie, Tony and Michael watch from the audience \u2014 the father overcome with astonishment and pride. The image asserts that the escape was worth its cost and that the family has come to witness rather than to forbid.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: Billy, your family are here. / Thanks.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The ending validates everything the film has argued for: acceptance letter, father's tears, the leap. Reception describes it as 'charming', 'very moving and very uplifting', 'as raw a slice of escapism as you could wish for', and Ebert calls it 'as much parable and fantasy as it is realistic' \u2014 no critic names irony. Homophobia, police violence and the strike's defeat are depicted critically but the film's own frame (Billy's) is adopted wholeheartedly.
interiority_granted: Mrs Wilkinson (partly \u2014 her frustrated ambition and unhappy marriage)
punished: the mining community, which loses the strike
Jackie, humiliated at the scab bus and forced to pawn his wife's jewellery
Mrs Wilkinson's husband Tom, made redundant
forgiven: Jackie, for the ban and for nearly crossing the picket line
Billy, for punching the boy at the audition
Tony, for his violence toward Billy and Mrs Wilkinson
Michael, whose difference is accepted rather than corrected
evidence_quotes: Lads do football or boxing or wrestling! Not frigging ballet.
Always be yourself. I love you forever.
Like there's fire in me body. I'm just there, flying. Like a bird. Like electricity.
Let's give the boy a fucking chance!
We're going back. Strike's over, Jackie. The union caved in yesterday.
This is when you go out and find life, and all those other things.

films.title: Gladiator
films.description: A respected leader loses everything and is drawn into a public struggle over revenge, honour, and the future of a nation.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: The film locates legitimate authority in a dying emperor's designated trust, exercised on behalf of the people and returned to the Senate — a republic restored by consent and by the virtue of an uncorrupted man. Inheritance by blood is explicitly rejected ('Commodus cannot rule. He must not rule.'), and force wielded for its own ends is illegitimate; earned merit plus renunciation of power is the mark of the legitimate holder.
skeleton.opening_power: Emperor Marcus Aurelius, an aging autocrat who has decided to hand his powers to General Maximus in trust; Maximus commands the army's loyalty.
skeleton.closing_power: Commodus and Maximus are both dead; Senator Gracchus is reinstated and the Praetorians obey Maximus' dying instruction — power passes to the Senate, with Lucilla and Lucius safe.
skeleton.what_is_restored: The republic Marcus Aurelius wished for — the Senate's authority, Gracchus reinstated, 'a dream that was Rome' — and Maximus' reunion with his family in the afterlife.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Hereditary imperial succession by blood; Commodus' line is extinguished and his rule by spectacle, terror and the mob is dismantled. The gladiators are freed.
skeleton.antagonist: Commodus
skeleton.antagonist_origin: A son who believed his father never loved him and never valued his virtues — 'I would butcher the whole world, if you would only have loved me!'
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: His wish to withdraw from public duty into private life — 'Let me go home' — and, after his family's murder, a vengeance-driven despair that makes him refuse the political trust ('With all my heart, no'; 'I am a slave! What possible difference can I make?').
skeleton.protagonist_change: He TAKES UP the burden handed to him by Marcus Aurelius, subordinating personal vengeance to the restoration of the republic — killing Commodus but dying having ordered the Senate reinstated and his men freed, refusing power for himself ('I will leave. The soldiers will stay for your protection, under the command of the Senate').
skeleton.final_image: Night in the emptied Colosseum: Juba buries the figurines of Maximus' wife and son in the sand where he died, saying he will see him again — the arena of spectacle converted into a private grave, and the hero's reward figured as reunion with family rather than rule.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: Now we are free. I will see you again. But not yet. Not yet.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The film's frame is unironically Maximus': his dying instructions are obeyed verbatim ('These are the wishes of Marcus Aurelius'), Lucilla's eulogy asks Rome to 'believe it again', and the score-and-elegy closing endorses him as 'a soldier of Rome'. Reception treats it as a sincere, even 'glum revenge story' with a 'bruised heart', criticising it as 'predictable and formulaic' and the dialogue as 'pompous' — nobody names irony or satire. Parenti's complaint that Romans are portrayed 'as bloodthirsty savages' is a complaint about sincere depiction, not detected critique. The arena spectacle is critiqued through Gracchus and Proximo, but the film's own heroic register is unqualified.
forgiven: Lucilla
Proximo
Quintus
Maximus (for his vengeance)
evidence_quotes: I want you to become the protector of Rome after I die... to give power back to the people of Rome
Commodus is not a moral man... Commodus cannot rule. He must not rule.
I would butcher the whole world, if you would only have loved me!
Rome is the mob. Conjure magic for them, and they'll be distracted.
I will not trade one dictatorship for another!
Senator Gracchus is to be reinstated. There was a dream that was Rome. It shall be realized. These are the wishes of Marcus Aurelius.

films.title: Shrek
films.description: A solitary outsider’s quiet life is interrupted by a quest that challenges his assumptions about beauty and belonging.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: The film locates legitimate authority in freely given love, chosen belonging and mutual acceptance rather than in title, law or force. Farquaad's route to kingship \u2014 acquiring a princess so a marriage contract will make him king ("you're not a king yet... All you have to do is marry a princess"; "This marriage is binding, and that makes me king!") \u2014 is treated as a fraud, and the magic mirror's procedural rule is played as a game show. Rule enforced by bounty, eviction and torture (the gingerbread man interrogation, the caged creatures sold for shillings) is illegitimate by the film's lights; the only authority the ending validates is the self-chosen bond between Shrek and Fiona.
skeleton.opening_power: Lord Farquaad rules Duloc, purging fairy-tale creatures with paid bounties, eviction notices and 'resettlement facilities'; Shrek holds only his swamp, by intimidation, and Fiona is held captive by the terms of a curse and a dragon.
skeleton.closing_power: Farquaad is devoured by Dragon mid-decree; Shrek and Fiona hold their own life in the swamp, married, with the fairy-tale creatures free and in attendance. The evidence never says who, if anyone, rules Duloc afterwards \u2014 the throne is simply vacated and dropped.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Shrek's swamp is returned to him by deed ('The deed to your swamp, cleared out, as agreed'), but the solitude he wanted with it is not: the ending shows the swamp full of guests. What is restored is the property, not the isolation.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Farquaad's regime of enforced 'perfection' and expulsion of the unlike; and the fairy-tale rule that the spell must resolve into conventional beauty \u2014 Fiona 'takes love's true form' by remaining an ogress ('I'm supposed to be beautiful.' / 'But you are beautiful.'). The princess-rescued-by-Prince-Charming template is dismantled rather than fulfilled.
skeleton.antagonist: Lord Farquaad of Duloc
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Defensive isolation \u2014 Shrek pre-emptively rejects everyone because he expects to be judged for what he looks like ('They judge me before they even know me. That's why I'm better off alone'), expressed literally as a plan to build a ten-foot wall, and compounded by his own habit of jumping to conclusions about Fiona.
skeleton.protagonist_change: He PUTS DOWN the armour of self-exile imposed on him by others' judgement \u2014 admitting 'I guess I am just a big, stupid, ugly ogre. Can you forgive me?', accepting friendship ('Friends.'), and saying 'I love you' in public. He takes up nothing handed to him by any authority: no title, no crown, no reward beyond the swamp he already owned; the change is the dropping of the wall.
skeleton.final_image: Per the evidence, the closing stretch is the wedding celebration in the swamp with the fairy-tale creatures singing 'I'm a Believer' and the couple departing; the asserted claim is that the ogress form is the true and beautiful one and that a community of the excluded, not a purified kingdom, is where happiness lives.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: But you are beautiful.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The irreverence is aimed at genre convention and at Farquaad, not at the film's own resolution, which is played straight: the critical consensus says it is 'simultaneously embracing and subverting fairy tales' while it 'manages to tweak Disney's nose, provide a moral message to children'; Ebert calls it 'jolly and wicked... and yet somehow possessing a heart'; Rodriguez says it 'never becomes cynical or crass'. Even the dissent (Lemire) concedes it 'strives to have a heart' with 'a message about beauty coming from within' \u2014 disputing execution, not sincerity. The declaration scene and the 'you are beautiful' beat carry no ironic undercutting in the dialogue.
skeleton.source_text: The children's book Shrek! by William Steig (named in the reception layer: 'based on the children's book by William Steig'; Steig and his wife are quoted approving the film).
skeleton.inverts_source_how: Against the fairy-tale template it quotes in its own opening narration ('She waited in the dragon's keep... for her true love and true love's first kiss' \u2014 immediately answered with 'Like that's ever gonna happen'), the film inverts the terms: the rescuer is the monster, the rescued princess is a fighter and secretly a monster herself, the courtly lord is the villain, the dragon is a lover and liberator, and the breaking of the spell confers ogre-hood rather than beauty.
interiority_withheld: the captured fairy-tale creatures (except the gingerbread man's brief scene)
punished: Robin Hood and his Merry Men
Shrek (temporarily, with misery and loneliness, for jumping to conclusions and driving Donkey away)
forgiven: Shrek
Donkey
Fiona (for her deception and for accepting Farquaad)
Dragon (who begins as the obstacle and ends as the rescuer)
unsupported_fields: closing_power (who governs Duloc after Farquaad's death is never stated)
final_spoken_line (the transcript's last spoken exchange is followed by song lyrics and an interjected 'God bless us, every one'; the true final line of the film cannot be settled with certainty)
evidence_quotes: Well, technically you're not a king.
I will make this Princess Fiona my queen, and DuLoc will finally have the perfect king!
I'm not the monster here. You are. You and the rest of that fairy tale trash, poisoning my perfect world.
They judge me before they even know me. That's why I'm better off alone.
Maybe you shouldn't judge people before you get to know them.

films.title: Spirited Away
films.description: A child in an unfamiliar world learns to hold onto compassion and identity amid rules she does not understand.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Not inheritance or law but contract honored, work performed, remembered true names, and reciprocal obligation; the film treats authority as legitimate only insofar as it keeps its word and does not steal identity — Yubaba rules by contract and name-theft, and is bound by 'that ridiculous oath I took / To give work to whoever asks' and by 'a rule's a rule'
skeleton.opening_power: Yubaba, the sorceress who owns and runs the bathhouse, holds absolute power over its workers through signed contracts and stolen names; in the human frame, Chihiro's parents hold power over her ('C'mon now, behave yourself')
skeleton.closing_power: Yubaba still owns and runs the bathhouse, but is forced by her own rules and her son's rebuke to release Chihiro; Chihiro holds her own name again and walks out; Haku quits his apprenticeship; Zeniba keeps her seal and takes in No-Face
skeleton.what_is_restored: Chihiro's name and her parents' human form; Haku's true name and identity as the Kohaku River spirit; the family's ordinary journey to the new house, resumed as if uninterrupted
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Yubaba's hold over Haku (the controlling slug is crushed, he quits), Chihiro's contract dissolves, and Chihiro's own timidity; No-Face is removed from the bathhouse's corrupting economy
skeleton.antagonist: Yubaba
skeleton.antagonist_origin: She is one of two halves of a whole — Zeniba says 'My sister and I are two halves of a whole, but we really don't get along' — and her greed and control are bound up with doting maternal attachment to her baby, which is what finally softens her
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Fearful, sulking, clinging passivity — she is called 'a lazy, spoiled, crybaby,' cannot stand when frightened, and clings to her mother
skeleton.protagonist_change: She becomes capable, insistent and self-possessed, working, thanking, and acting for others; crucially she PUTS DOWN the imposed name 'Sen' and reclaims 'Chihiro' — she takes up nothing that is handed to her except Zeniba's hairband, and refuses the offered gold
skeleton.final_image: Chihiro, still wearing Zeniba's hairband, pauses and looks back at the dusty tunnel her parents dismiss as 'some kind of joke,' then goes on with them to the new house — the ordinary world resumed, but with the girl changed and holding a secret
skeleton.final_spoken_line: Hurry up, Chihiro!
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The film depicts the bathhouse economy — gold-begging, name-stealing, contract servitude — at length while plainly condemning it: the analysis notes 'it is a place of excess and greed,' Yubaba's Western dress and décor represent 'the Western capitalist influence over Japan,' and Miyazaki states 'Chihiro's parents turning into pigs symbolizes how some humans become greedy.' The greedy are punished, the gold is refused ('I don't want any Don't need any'), and No-Face becomes gentle only once removed from the bathhouse.
punished: Chihiro's parents (turned into pigs for gorging)
the greedy bathhouse workers swallowed by No-Face
Yubaba (loses her fortune, her hold on Haku, and is scolded by her own son)
forgiven: Haku ('I no longer blame you for what you did')
No-Face (taken in by Zeniba)
Chihiro's parents (restored, though they never learn what happened)

That ridiculous oath I took / To give work to whoever asks
Anyone can see you're a lazy, spoiled, crybaby

films.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
films.description: Ordinary companions carry a burden through a collapsing world while leaders decide what power is for.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Inherited bloodline confirmed by prophecy and sacred token — the heir of Elendil wielding the reforged sword — plus proven virtue (mercy, courage, refusal of the Ring). Stewardship is explicitly a lesser, custodial thing; the film says 'Lord Denethor, however, is not king. He is a steward only, a caretaker of the throne.' Oaths sworn and kept are the other binding source of legitimacy.
skeleton.opening_power: Sauron, whose armies dominate Middle-earth; Denethor rules Gondor as steward and Théoden rules Rohan; Aragorn is an uncrowned Ranger in exile. Saruman is already defeated and locked in his tower.
skeleton.closing_power: Aragorn, crowned King of Gondor, married to Arwen; the Age of Men begins ('The time has come for the dominion of Men'). In the Shire, Sam is a settled householder. The Elves and Gandalf depart, ceding the world to Men.
skeleton.what_is_restored: The line of kings and the throne of Gondor; the White Tree flowers again; the Shire's ordinary domestic life; the oath-breaking Dead are released once their pledge is honoured.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Sauron and the Ring are destroyed forever; the rule of the Stewards ends with Denethor's death; the age of the Elves and the power of the Three Rings ends, and Frodo cannot re-enter the life he saved.
skeleton.antagonist: Sauron, with Gollum as the intimate antagonist and the Witch-king as his field commander; Denethor and Saruman as lesser obstructive authorities.
skeleton.antagonist_origin: Gollum is shown in a prologue as the hobbit Sméagol, an ordinary creature immediately ensnared by the Ring who murders his cousin and is then cursed, driven away and hollowed out by it ('We even forgot our own name'); Denethor's cruelty is framed by grief for Boromir.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Frodo: the Ring's corrosive weight, which turns him suspicious of the friend who loves him and finally makes him claim the Ring for himself. Aragorn: reluctance to claim his inheritance, hiding in the Ranger. Sam: nothing but doubt about his own smallness. Éowyn: being denied a part in the fight.
skeleton.protagonist_change: Aragorn TAKES UP what is handed to him — the reforged sword, the crown, the throne ('Put aside the Ranger. Become who you were born to be'). Frodo does not overcome the Ring by will; he is saved by Sam's fidelity and Gollum's greed, and at the end PUTS DOWN the burden entirely, leaving Middle-earth. Sam takes up the book and the ongoing life.
skeleton.final_image: Sam returns from the Grey Havens to Bag End, is met by Rosie and their two children, steps inside and closes the door — domestic continuity asserted as the reward the war purchased, set against Frodo's ship vanishing into the West.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: Well I'm back.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The film unambiguously validates its own hierarchy: the coronation is scored as triumph, 'Now come the days of the king. May they be blessed,' and the crowned king tells the hobbits 'you bow to no one.' Reception confirms sincerity — critics call it 'emotionally powerful,' 'moving and satisfying,' with the only ironic reading coming from a dissenting critic (Romney) complaining of 'self-important solemnity' and 'beautiful Europeans boldly fending off the nameless, numberless hordes' — i.e. the film's earnestness is what he objects to, not a satirical stance it holds.
skeleton.source_text: J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings
forgiven: Pippin (for looking into the palantír — 'A fool but an honest fool he remains')
Frodo (for casting out Sam and for claiming the Ring)
Faramir
the Dead, whose oath is held fulfilled
Boromir by implication

Authority is not given to you to deny the return of the king, steward.
Put aside the Ranger. Become who you were born to be.
I am Isildur's heir. Fight for me and I will hold your oaths fulfilled.

films.title: V for Vendetta
films.description: A citizen living under fearful rule is invited to consider whether liberation can be separated from violence and revenge.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Consent of the governed and individual integrity — the film treats authority as legitimate only when the people are not ruled by fear; V's line 'People should not be afraid of their governments. Governments should be afraid of their people' is offered without rebuttal, and Valerie's 'inch' of inviolable personal integrity is the moral bedrock. Legitimacy is explicitly denied to power obtained by manufactured fear and fraud.
skeleton.opening_power: The Norsefire party — High Chancellor Adam Sutler, with Creedy's secret police (Fingermen), Prothero's propaganda apparatus and a compliant state broadcaster — rules Britain absolutely.
skeleton.closing_power: No one clearly. Sutler and Creedy are dead, the military stands down of its own accord ('No response from Command... Or from the high chancellor'), Parliament is destroyed, and an unarmed masked crowd occupies the streets. Power is left with an undifferentiated 'us' and an unspecified future: 'tomorrow, a different world will begin that different people will shape.'
skeleton.what_is_restored: Almost nothing of the prior order; what is recovered is memory and the suppressed past — the meaning of the 5th of November, the banned art, music and books of the Shadow Gallery, Valerie's letter, the truth about Larkhill and St. Mary's.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: The Norsefire regime and its founding lie: the fabricated terrorist attack, the sale of the cure, the machinery of curfew, censorship, black bags and detention camps. Parliament itself is destroyed as the symbol of that order, and the ruling clique is killed.
skeleton.antagonist: High Chancellor Adam Sutler and Party Leader Peter Creedy (Norsefire)
skeleton.antagonist_origin: Sutler is described as a 'young, up-and-coming politician... deeply religious... completely single-minded' whose party's biological weapons project produced a virus that Creedy — 'a man seemingly without a conscience for whom the ends always justify the means' — proposed turning on Britain itself to seize power; the account explains their rise but is offered as indictment rather than mitigation.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Fear. Evey is governed by it — 'Sorry I'm not a stronger person... I wish I wasn't afraid all the time but I am' — and complies with a regime that killed her family.
skeleton.protagonist_change: She loses her fear through the fabricated imprisonment ('Then you have no fear anymore. You're completely free') and TAKES UP what V hands her: his home, his gallery, the train and the decision to pull the lever. She also PUTS DOWN the imposed compliance and anonymity of her old life; she chooses to detonate, then speaks for V's meaning ('He was all of us').
skeleton.final_image: Parliament and Big Ben exploding to the 1812 Overture while a vast crowd of unmasked citizens — the masks lowered — watches, intercut with the faces of the dead (Valerie, Gordon, Delia, Evey's parents); Evey's voiceover asserts that the man, not only the idea, is what should be remembered. The image asserts that the tyranny is finished and that the act was collective and justified.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: No one will ever forget that night and what it meant for this country. But I will never forget the man and what he meant to me.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The telling adopts V's frame throughout: his broadcast argument goes unanswered, his victims are shown to be torturers, profiteers and child abusers, the regime's own dialogue is nakedly self-incriminating ('Our job is to report the news, not fabricate it. That's the government's job'), the investigating policeman is converted and stands down, and the closing voiceover is an elegy for V. Reception confirms the film is read as sincere advocacy rather than critique — Roeper notes the 'terrorist' label is applied 'by someone who's essentially Hitler,' Graeber says 'the message of anarchy got out,' and the socialist critic Walsh attacks the film precisely for endorsing 'anarcho-terrorist ideology' rather than for satirising it. Criticism of the politics as 'adolescent stuff' is criticism of an earnest position, not detection of irony.
skeleton.source_text: Alan Moore and David Lloyd's comic V for Vendetta (Moore removed his name from the film); also invokes the historical Guy Fawkes / Gunpowder Plot and Dumas's The Count of Monte Cristo, Shakespeare's Macbeth, Richard III and Twelfth Night, and Faust.
skeleton.inverts_source_how: It inverts the historical memory of Guy Fawkes: the rhyme's traitor whose failure is annually celebrated becomes a hero whose plot succeeds and is vindicated. Reception indicates the comic's anarchist message was also altered — anarchists protested that the film 'watered down the story's original message in favour of violence and special effects' and that 'creating communities and democratic decision making... is absent from Hollywood's interpretation' — but the evidence does not specify further inversions of the source.

films.title: No Country for Old Men
films.description: A chance discovery pulls several people into a pursuit where chance, violence, and moral certainty seem increasingly unstable.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: The film locates legitimate authority in an inherited lineage of lawmen — sheriffs, fathers and grandfathers who kept order by presence and decency rather than force ('Some of the old-time sheriffs never even wore a gun') — and then shows that authority as obsolete and unable to answer the violence now in the world; no other legitimate source replaces it, only chance, force and Chigurh's private 'principles'.
skeleton.opening_power: Nominally the law — Sheriff Ed Tom Bell narrating over Chigurh's arrest, a deputy saying 'I got it under control' — but effectively Chigurh, who kills the deputy within minutes; drug money and its owners move underneath.
skeleton.closing_power: Chigurh, injured but free and unpunished, walking away from the crash; the law has withdrawn — Bell is retired, sitting at his kitchen table recounting a dream.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Nothing. The money is dispersed, the killer uncaught, the murdered are not avenged; only Bell's private domesticity remains.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: The Wild West narrative of the lawman who masters evil: Bell's inherited vocation is put down, the badge retired, and the belief that violence can be understood or contained is dismantled.
skeleton.antagonist: Anton Chigurh
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Bell's assumption that he can comprehend and match the evil in front of him — and the vanity Ellis names in thinking events wait on him; (Moss, the other protagonist, is undone by greed and by the pride of a man who 'never thinks he needs any' help).
skeleton.protagonist_change: Bell PUTS DOWN the office handed to him by father and grandfather — he retires, admitting 'I feel overmatched' — and accepts detachment; what replaces the flaw is not mastery but a resigned, unconsoled acceptance figured in the dream of his father going on ahead with fire.
skeleton.final_image: Bell, retired, at the breakfast table telling his wife two dreams of his dead father — the lost money, and the father riding ahead through cold and dark carrying fire in a horn to build a campfire — then a cut to black; it asserts that the only remaining good is inherited memory and a hoped-for light beyond the present darkness, not any victory over it.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: Then, I woke up.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: Reception frames the violence as condemned rather than relished: 'No Country for Old Men doesn't celebrate or smile at violence; it despairs of it'; Joel Coen calls it 'a character confronting a very arbitrary violent brutal world, and you have to see that.' The analysis also treats Chigurh's fatalism as bad faith — he 'hands responsibility over to fate in an act of bad faith that prevents him from taking responsibility' — and Carla Jean's 'The coin don't have no say. It's just you' refuses his code from inside the film. The film depicts an order of implacable violence without validating it, while also withholding any triumph from the law.
skeleton.source_text: No Country for Old Men (2005 novel) by Cormac McCarthy
interiority_granted: Ed Tom Bell (opening narration, the confession to Ellis, the closing dream)
Llewelyn Moss (partially — his reasoning, his guilt in returning with water)
Carla Jean (her refusal of the coin toss)
interiority_withheld: the businessman/accountant who hires the hunters
punished: the truck driver, motel clerk and other bystanders
forgiven: the gas station owner (spared by the coin)

films.title: The Dark Knight
films.description: A protector faces an enemy who believes fear can reveal what every decent person is really willing to do.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: The film locates legitimate authority in elected/legal institutions — the DA's office, the courts, the police commissioner — but treats that legitimacy as insufficient in emergency, requiring an unelected, self-appointed protector who operates outside law and a 'noble lie' told by a small group to sustain public faith. Consent and law are named as the ideal ('this is a democracy, Harvey'); competence, sacrifice and symbolic function are what the ending actually rewards.
skeleton.opening_power: Formally: Mayor, Commissioner Loeb, judges and the new DA Harvey Dent; informally: the mafia families (Maroni, Gambol, the Chechen) with Lau holding their money, and Batman operating as an extralegal check. The Joker is an unknown quantity robbing a mob bank.
skeleton.closing_power: Gordon as commissioner and the surviving legal order, sustained by a manufactured myth of Harvey Dent as martyr; Batman voluntarily exiled and hunted; the Joker captured but alive and unbroken; the mob dismantled.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Public faith in Gotham's institutions and in Dent's prosecutions — preserved by concealment rather than by fact. Batman's rule against killing is upheld with the Joker; the surveillance apparatus is dismantled and the pre-emergency ethical boundary re-established.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Dent's idealism and the possibility of a legitimate, public, law-abiding hero; Batman's status as an accepted protector — he becomes a hunted criminal by choice; the mob's financial power; the truth itself, permanently replaced by an official lie both Gordon and Alfred are complicit in.
skeleton.antagonist: The Joker (with Harvey Dent / Two-Face as the second, created antagonist)
skeleton.antagonist_origin: The Joker offers mutually contradictory accounts of his scars — an abusive father, then a disfigured wife — and the film explicitly denies him identity or record ('No matches on prints, DNA, dental... No name'), so no backstory is supplied as true. Dent, by contrast, is given a fully explanatory origin: Rachel's death and his disfigurement.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Bruce Wayne's belief that Batman can be temporary and can have no limits — that he can hand the burden to Dent, retire into a private life with Rachel, and that no cost attaches to his escalation ('Batman has no limits' / 'Did I bring this on her?').
skeleton.protagonist_change: He accepts limits and permanence at once: he refuses to kill, destroys the surveillance machine, and TAKES UP an imposed burden — the blame for Dent's murders and the role of hunted villain — rather than putting anything down. He surrenders the private life he wanted and chooses to be 'whatever Gotham needs me to be.'
skeleton.final_image: Batman fleeing on the Batpod, pursued by police dogs and squad cars, over Gordon's voiceover explaining to his son that they must chase him — the hero deliberately converted into a fugitive so a lie can hold the city together. The image asserts that sacrifice without recognition is the highest civic virtue.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: He's a silent guardian a watchful protector. A Dark Knight.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The film's own summation is delivered without irony by the most virtuous character, Gordon, in reverent voiceover, and Batman states the doctrine plainly: 'sometimes the truth isn't good enough. Sometimes people deserve more.' The themes section notes 'Although The Dark Knight presents this as a heroic act, this "noble lie" is used to conceal and manipulate the truth,' and that McGowan 'considered the act heroic' — i.e. critics import the critique, the film asserts the heroism. Reception is genuinely split ('a perfect mirror of the society which is watching it'), and the film does undercut itself once — Fox's resignation over surveillance, and the fact that Batman's escalation created the Joker — but the ending validates rather than ironises the deception.
skeleton.source_text: Batman comic books (DC Comics); direct sequel to an earlier film in the same series (Wayne Manor being rebuilt, Falcone in Arkham).
interiority_withheld: The ferry prisoner who throws the detonator overboard
forgiven: Harvey Dent (posthumously, by the lie that canonises him)
Ramirez (spared by Dent: 'You live to fight another day, officer')
Gordon (absolved by Batman assuming his guilt)
The ferry passengers and prisoners
Bruce Wayne (by Alfred burning Rachel's letter)

films.title: WALL-E
films.description: A lonely caretaker discovers connection and asks a comfortable society to remember what responsibility to a shared world requires.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: The film locates legitimate authority in living, choosing agents who accept responsibility for stewardship of the world — the human captain reclaiming command from an automated directive, and love/'irrational' choice overriding programming. Obedience to an inherited corporate order (BnL's directive A113) is treated as illegitimate precisely because it is a dead instruction outliving the conditions that produced it: 'Auto, things have changed!'; 'I don't want to survive. I want to live!'
skeleton.opening_power: Buy n Large's automated legacy: the megacorporation's 700-year-old programming, executed aboard the Axiom by the autopilot AUTO, with the nominal Captain a figurehead and humanity passive in hoverchairs; on Earth, no one — only abandoned machines and refuse.
skeleton.closing_power: Captain McCrea and the human passengers, now standing and acting on Earth, with robots working alongside them; AUTO deactivated and BnL's directive void.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Humanity's presence on Earth, walking on soil; farming, dancing, gathering, the nuclear-family/community life evoked by 'Put on Your Sunday Clothes'; WALL-E's erased personality and memory; his relationship with EVE.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: The BnL order itself — the classified no-return directive A113, the hoverchair regime of automated care, AUTO's rule; humanity's passivity ('That's all I've ever done... Nothing!') is permanently exchanged for labor and stewardship.
skeleton.antagonist: AUTO, the autopilot, executing Shelby Forthright/Buy n Large's directive A113 (with GO-4 as its enforcer)
skeleton.antagonist_origin: AUTO was given a secret standing order in 2110 by BnL's CEO — 'I'm giving Override Directive A 113... do not return to Earth' — after Operation Cleanup failed, and it has simply never stopped obeying an instruction whose premise has expired.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: For WALL-E, isolation and mere routine — compaction, collection, loneliness — a life of programmed function without connection; for the Captain, inherited passivity and incuriosity, presiding over 'unchanged' reports and doing nothing.
skeleton.protagonist_change: WALL-E puts down his imposed directive and risks himself for love, persisting past erasure; the Captain TAKES UP the command handed to him by circumstance — literally rising from the hoverchair onto his own feet ('I'm the captain of the Axiom. We are going home today.' / 'Auto, you are relieved of duty.') and accepts the burden of stewardship. Both are cases of putting down a programmed instruction and taking up chosen responsibility.
skeleton.final_image: Humans and robots working the ravaged Earth together — 'This is called farming!... Pizza plants!' / 'It's good to be home!' — and, over the credits song, the seedling growing into a tree that WALL-E and EVE admire; the closing assertion is renewal through labor and care: 'the land will be looked after / We'll send the seeds out in the breeze.'
skeleton.final_spoken_line: It's good to be home!
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The film sincerely endorses its ending (return, work, love), but the consumer order it depicts at length — BnL jingles, hoverchairs, 'B is for Buy n Large, your very best friend', 'lunch in a cup' — is satirized, not endorsed. Reception confirms the critical intent: it is 'recognized as a social criticism'; Kyle Smith called it 'darker and more cynical than any major Disney feature'; conservative critics read it as 'a 90-minute lecture on the dangers of over consumption, big corporations'; Gilliam praised 'all the people on their loungers floating around... Their social comment was so smart.' The endorsement itself is unironic: AFI's citation and the closing credits song treat the return to Earth straight.
skeleton.inverts_source_how: Per the film's commentators, EVE's namesake is inverted: where the biblical Eve occasions expulsion from the garden, this EVE's plant summons humanity back to Earth and away from the 'false god' of BnL; she is also glossed as the dove returning with an olive branch to end the voyage.

punished: the Buy n Large order and its consumer regime
implicitly the passengers, whose complacency has cost them their bodies
forgiven: EVE, for having WALL-E designated rogue and for her earlier directive-bound rigidity
the human passengers, who are shown joining the effort rather than blamed

films.title: A Separation
films.description: A family dispute becomes a web of competing duties, where every honest choice appears to harm someone else.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: The film locates legitimate authority in truth-telling verified by conscience and religious oath rather than in the courts; state law (family court, criminal judge, blood money) is depicted as procedurally binding but incapable of resolving moral questions, and the decisive moment is Razieh's refusal to swear on the Qur'an — private conscience overrides both legal settlement and patriarchal command
skeleton.opening_power: Nader holds domestic authority (refuses permission for wife and daughter to emigrate, and the court upholds his veto); the family court judge holds procedural power and dismisses Simin's petition as 'a small problem'
skeleton.closing_power: Neither parent; the marriage is legally dissolved and the decision is displaced onto the child — Termeh alone, before a judge, chooses which parent she will live with, while both wait outside
skeleton.what_is_restored: Nothing is restored; the household never reassembles and the wandering father, the lost pregnancy and the lost job all stand
skeleton.what_is_overturned: The marriage is dissolved; Nader's earlier claim to be the injured innocent is dismantled by his own confession that he lied; the poorer couple's claim collapses under Razieh's conscience, leaving them without the settlement money; the parental authority that framed the opening scene is handed to the child
skeleton.antagonist: No single antagonist — Hodjat functions as the pressing adversary, but the film distributes fault across Nader, Simin, Razieh and Hodjat alike
skeleton.antagonist_origin: Hodjat is a cobbler fired after ten years who sued and lost, is jailed repeatedly by creditors, is on medication for depression, and says 'I have nothing to lose'
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Nader's pride and inflexibility — refusal to concede fault, willingness to lie under oath to avoid prison, treating settlement as extortion rather than responsibility; Simin's counterpart flaw is the wish to solve everything by leaving or paying
skeleton.protagonist_change: Nader puts down the lie — he confesses to Termeh that he heard the conversation and knew of the pregnancy, and later insists on the Qur'anic oath rather than buying silence; he takes up nothing new, and gains no vindication, since the confession costs him his daughter's trust and the divorce proceeds
skeleton.final_image: Termeh alone with the judge saying she has decided but asking that her parents wait outside; then a long held shot of Nader and Simin waiting apart in the corridor — the answer withheld from the audience
skeleton.final_spoken_line: Sir, wait outside for a minute. You too, ma'am.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The telling is sincere and even-handed rather than ironic: critics describe it as 'morally complex', with 'a feel for ethical nuance', raising 'questions of responsibility, of the subjectivity and contingency of "telling the truth"'; Thomson notes 'you cannot watch the film without feeling kinship with the characters and admitting their decency as well as their mistakes'. It withholds judgement rather than staging a critique it disowns — though the courtroom scenes clearly present the legal machinery as inadequate ('My finding is that your problem is a small problem')

forgiven: Razieh, whose refusal to swear is treated as integrity rather than deceit
Hodjat, whose violence is contextualised by unemployment, debt and illness

films.title: Les Misérables
films.description: Lives collide across years as mercy, law, poverty, and a chance to become someone new pull in different directions.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Divine grace and mercy rather than law: authority is legitimate insofar as it serves love and the suffering poor. The Bishop's unearned forgiveness ('God has raised you out of darkness / I have saved your soul for God') is the film's origin of moral authority; legal authority ('My duty is to the law') is shown as rigid, self-destroying and finally invalid. Popular revolt against the monarchy is treated sympathetically but as prophecy rather than as an accomplished mandate.
skeleton.opening_power: The French penal state — the prison at Toulon and its guards, Javert enforcing parole; the restored monarchy and the propertied class above the destitute poor.
skeleton.closing_power: Politically unchanged: the state crushed the barricade and 'the people of Paris sleep in their beds'; Marius and Cosette are married into the bourgeoisie (a wedding with a Baron title in attendance). Moral authority rests with Valjean's example, and the final chorus asserts a future popular liberation not yet achieved.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Valjean's name and honor (openly 'Jean Valjean' again rather than 24601), his reunion with Cosette, and family order via the marriage; the state's control of the streets is restored after the revolt.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Javert's absolutist equation of law with justice is destroyed from within — he cannot survive having been forgiven; and Valjean's identity as convict is permanently dissolved into sainthood ('Cosette, your father is a saint').
skeleton.antagonist: Javert (with the Thénardiers as secondary predators)
skeleton.antagonist_origin: Javert declares he was born in a jail among 'scum' and rose by absolute obedience to law — 'I was born inside a jail! I was born with scum like you! I am from the gutter, too!'
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Hatred and the desire for vengeance born of nineteen years' injustice — 'Take an eye for an eye! Turn your heart into stone! This is all I have lived for' — plus the fear-driven concealment and possessiveness that make him hide his past and nearly take Cosette away.
skeleton.protagonist_change: He TAKES UP the burden handed to him by the Bishop — a purchased soul and the obligation to 'become an honest man' — and repeatedly takes up further imposed duties (confessing at the trial, raising Cosette, sparing Javert, carrying Marius); at the end he PUTS DOWN both his secret and his claim on Cosette, surrendering her to Marius and dying: 'Monsieur, lay down your burden.'
skeleton.final_image: Valjean dies attended by the spirits of Fantine and the Bishop and is led into an afterlife where the barricade dead — Éponine, Gavroche, Enjolras and the students — stand on an immense barricade waving the tricolor, singing 'Do you hear the people sing... It is the future that we bring when tomorrow comes!' The image asserts that private love and collective liberation are the same salvation, deferred to a promised future.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: Do you hear the people sing? Say, do you hear the distant drums? It is the future that we bring when tomorrow comes!
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: Everything is played at full emotional pitch and rewarded as sincere: the dying Valjean is canonized ('Cosette, your father is a saint'), the closing maxim is delivered without irony ('To love another person is to see the face of God'), and reception describes it as 'a masterful tale of redemption, forgiveness, and love' and complains only of excess sincerity — 'bombastic', 'melodrama of it all soaring', 'everything... cranked to 11'. No critic identifies irony or satire; the barricade song's later real-world use as protest confirms the film plays it straight.
skeleton.source_text: The stage musical Les Misérables, from Victor Hugo's novel — reception calls it 'adapting a sprawling musical theater epic, which in turn is based on an even more sprawling and longwinded Victor Hugo novel'.

interiority_withheld: The soldiers and the army command
punished: Enjolras and the Friends of the ABC

Fantine

films.title: Frozen
films.description: Two sisters must choose between a safe distance and the difficult honesty required to repair a family bond.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Inherited royal succession, but only when validated by the people's acceptance and by the ruler's self-mastery: Elsa is legitimate as the crowned heir ('Queen Elsa of Arendelle'), loses the court's consent when she is called 'Monster' and 'a wicked sorceress,' and regains rule when she can control her power through love. Claims through marriage ('I knew I would have to marry into the throne somewhere'), through accusation of witchcraft, or through commercial exploitation ('unlock your secrets and exploit your riches') are all treated as illegitimate.
skeleton.opening_power: The king and queen of Arendelle, who set the policy of concealment ('We'll lock the gates... keep her powers hidden from everyone'); after their deaths in a shipwreck, the crown passes to Elsa, who is crowned in the first act.
skeleton.closing_power: Elsa, restored and accepted as queen, ruling openly with Anna beside her; Kristoff installed by her appointment as 'Official Arendelle Ice Master and Deliverer'; Weselton stripped of trade and Hans deported.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Elsa's rightful place on the throne, the sisters' childhood closeness, summer, and the monarchy itself — the same family holds power at the end as at the beginning.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: The parental regime of concealment and isolation. The closed gates, the gloves and the doctrine 'Conceal, don't feel' are dismantled permanently: 'I like the open gates.' / 'We are never closing them again.' Also overturned: the belief that romantic love at first sight is 'true love.'
skeleton.antagonist: Prince Hans of the Southern Isles (with the Duke of Weselton as a secondary opportunist)
skeleton.antagonist_origin: Thirteenth of thirteen brothers with no prospect of a throne at home and three siblings who treated him as invisible for two years, so he set out to marry into a crown elsewhere.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Split between two protagonists: Elsa's fear of her own power and the conviction that isolation is the only way to keep others safe ('I belong here. Alone. Where I can be who I am without hurting anybody'); Anna's loneliness-driven naivety, throwing herself at a stranger ('You can't marry a man you just met').
skeleton.protagonist_change: Elsa learns that love, not suppression, controls the power ('Love will thaw... Love. Of course') and TAKES UP the crown and public role she had fled, while PUTTING DOWN the gloves and secrecy imposed on her by her parents. Anna PUTS DOWN the fantasy of instant romance and acts sacrificially instead ('You sacrificed yourself for me?'), earning a relationship she chose rather than one she fell into.
skeleton.final_image: The castle gates standing open, the courtyard turned to ice by Elsa's power for public play, the sisters skating together with Kristoff, Sven and Olaf. It asserts that the very faculty once hidden as monstrous is now a civic gift, and that legitimate rule is open rather than sealed.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: That's it, Olaf. Glide and pivot. And glide and pivot.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The film sincerely endorses everything its ending arranges: the sacrifice is validated literally by magic ('An act of true love will thaw a frozen heart'), and reception describes 'themes of self-acceptance and sacrifice' resonating and 'the film's positive messages,' with the only dissent (Lemire's 'cynical ... attempt to shake things up without shaking them up too much') being a complaint about timidity, not a claim of irony. The one thing held at ironic distance is the love-at-first-sight convention, which the film sets up and then demolishes via Hans's reveal — a 'reasonably surprising third-act twist' that the Writers Guild Foundation praised as subverting 'rigidly established story and character tropes.' That irony is aimed at a genre convention, not at the film's own moral order.

Anna ('For the First Time in Forever' gives her private hopes and loneliness)
Kristoff ('Reindeers Are Better Than People' gives his misanthropy and solitude)
Olaf ('In Summer' gives his innocent longing)

films.title: The Wolf of Wall Street
films.description: An ambitious newcomer embraces a culture of excess and must decide whether success excuses the damage left behind.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: The film locates real, effective authority not in law but in persuasive competence and appetite: the ability to sell, recruit and enrich oneself. Legal authority (SEC, FBI, the courts) exists and eventually acts, but is depicted as slow, bribable-adjacent and finally lenient — a 36-month sentence reduced to 22 months served, after which the same skill set is legitimately monetized again onstage. The frame the telling adopts is the protagonist's, in which making oneself rich is self-justifying ('their goal is to make themselves rich').
skeleton.opening_power: Established Wall Street firms and their senior brokers — L.F. Rothschild and Mark Hanna, who initiates the twenty-two-year-old Belfort into a drug-fueled culture whose stated purpose is self-enrichment; Belfort is a powerless entrant, and the market itself (Black Monday) then destroys his job.
skeleton.closing_power: Belfort again, in reduced but intact form: released from a minimum-security prison after 22 months and making a living hosting seminars on sales techniques, running the same recruitment test he used on his founding partners; per reception, the real Belfort appears beside a sign advertising his motivational-speaking company. Federal prosecutors hold formal power but have delivered only a token penalty.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Belfort's role as teacher of the pitch — the same sales test, the same rhetoric, a new roomful of listeners. The cycle that opened with Hanna instructing Belfort closes with Belfort instructing others.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Stratton Oakmont is raided and shut down; the fortune is exposed and the Swiss laundering collapses; Belfort's marriage ends with Naomi taking full custody; several associates (Brad, Saurel, Koskoff, and those he informs on) are arrested. His institutional apparatus is dismantled even though he personally is not.
skeleton.antagonist: FBI agent Denham (with the SEC and federal prosecution behind him) — the obstacle in the protagonist's frame; the film's other antagonist is Belfort's own appetite
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Insatiability — greed, drug addiction, and above all the inability to stop or step away, dramatized when, mid-farewell speech, he 'cannot bear to quit and talks himself into staying,' against his father's and lawyer's advice.
skeleton.protagonist_change: Essentially none that holds. He briefly attempts sobriety after the plane and yacht disasters, relapses after Naomi leaves, betrays his own cooperation deal by warning Donnie, serves 22 months, and then TAKES UP again the very instrument handed to him at the start — the hard sell — now as a paid instructor. He puts down nothing; what was imposed (prison, exposure) is simply outlasted.
skeleton.final_image: Belfort out of prison and back in front of an audience, running his old recruitment test at a sales seminar; per reception the real Belfort introduces him beneath a sign advertising his motivational-speaking company. The image asserts continuity rather than reckoning: the pitch survives the punishment, and there is always another room of people who want to learn it.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: Genuinely contested in the supplied evidence and not settled by it. For critique: the consensus calls the film 'Funny, self-referential, and irreverent to a fault,' and DiCaprio 'defended the film, arguing that it does not glorify the excessive lifestyle it depicts'; the CinemaScore 'C' and the note that marketing 'may have attracted conservative viewers who expected a more moralistic tone' imply the film withholds moralizing rather than approving. Against: 'Some critics viewed the film as an irresponsible glorification of Belfort and his associates rather than a satirical takedown'; the finance-worker audience 'cheered' at the coke-stash scene; the prosecutor called the ending 'beyond an insult' for its 'positive depiction of Belfort uttering variants of the same falsehoods'; and Christina McDowell faults it for 'giving celebrity status to people who do not deserve it.' The structural fact is that the film withholds the victims entirely and grants only the perpetrator a voice — which reads as ironic self-indictment or as endorsement depending on the viewer.
skeleton.source_text: Jordan Belfort's memoir ('the film and the book on which it is based')

interiority_withheld: The thousands of defrauded investors, who are not depicted at all
Donnie Azoff (seen in behavior, not inhabited)
punished: Donnie Azoff and the Stratton colleagues Belfort informs on
Jordan Belfort, lightly — 22 months served, firm shut down, marriage and custody lost
forgiven: Jordan Belfort — granted leniency for testimony despite breaching his deal, released, and permitted a second public career

films.title: Maleficent
films.description: A feared outsider revisits the betrayal that shaped her and discovers care in an unexpected bond.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Self-determination and mutual trust rather than inheritance or conquest; the Moors 'needed neither king nor queen, but trusted in one another,' and human kingship acquired by violence and ambition is shown as illegitimate — Maleficent tells King Henry 'You are no king to me.' Legitimate rule at the close is conferred by love and by the wronged party's own bestowal (Maleficent crowning Aurora), and validated by consent/unification.
skeleton.opening_power: Two kingdoms: a 'vain and greedy king' (Henry) ruling the human realm, and Maleficent as the strongest fairy and protector of the kingless, self-governing Moors.
skeleton.closing_power: Aurora crowned queen of a unified realm; Maleficent has removed her wall and 'took off her crown,' restored the Moors and stands beside Aurora rather than above her.
skeleton.what_is_restored: The Moors as they were 'once, long ago, when Maleficent was but a child and her heart was bright' — the wall of thorns comes down, the land is healed, and Maleficent's wings are returned to her body.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: The line of kings founded on mutilation and conquest — Stefan's dynasty ends with him; the border enmity between human kingdom and Moors is dissolved into a single unified kingdom; and the received version of the tale itself is overturned ('the story is not quite as you were told').
skeleton.antagonist: King Stefan
skeleton.antagonist_origin: An orphaned peasant thief who 'lived in a barn' and dreamed of the castle, whose ambition to be king overtook his love for Maleficent and who was promised the crown by the dying King Henry in exchange for her death.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Hatred and vengefulness born of betrayal and mutilation — she becomes 'lost in hatred and revenge,' rules the Moors bitterly, curses an innocent child, and denies that true love exists.
skeleton.protagonist_change: She recovers the capacity to love and takes responsibility for the harm she did ('what I have done to you is unforgivable'); crucially she PUTS DOWN what she seized — she removes the wall of thorns and 'took off her crown,' handing rule to Aurora — while taking back what was stolen from her (her wings) rather than accepting anything newly conferred.
skeleton.final_image: The elderly Aurora narrates over the united kingdom; the crown passes to her, Maleficent flies restored, and the telling reframes the villain of legend as 'one who was both hero and villain.'
skeleton.final_spoken_line: In the end, my kingdom was united not by a hero or a villain, as legend had predicted, but by one who was both hero and villain. And her name was Maleficent.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The narration and ending sincerely validate Maleficent's arc: 'her heart was bright. For now, it was again,' and the closing line canonises her as hero-and-villain. Reception treats it as an earnest revision, not satire — 'Long live the feminist revisionist backstory'; Jolie states the wing-removal 'was a metaphor for rape' and that the film is about 'how the abused then have a choice of abusing others or overcoming and remaining loving.' The one dissent (Bartyzel) faults it as a 'rape revenge fantasy' that is 'less feminist,' i.e. a complaint about the film's sincere position, not evidence of irony.
skeleton.source_text: Sleeping Beauty (the fairy tale, and specifically Disney's 1959 animated film — the framing 'Let us tell an old story anew, and we will see how well you know it')
skeleton.inverts_source_how: The wicked fairy becomes the wronged protagonist and true parent-figure; the heroic king becomes the mutilator and villain; 'true love's kiss' is stripped from the prince — whose kiss fails — and relocated to maternal love between the curser and the cursed; and the narrator is revealed as Sleeping Beauty correcting the legend.
interiority_granted: Aurora (who is also the retrospective narrator)
Diaval (partially, through his objections and loyalty)
punished: the pixies (scolded, mocked, left comic and ineffectual)
forgiven: Maleficent
Aurora
