films.title: Arrival
films.description: A specialist confronting the unknown learns that understanding another perspective may change how a life is valued.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Comprehension and freely given cooperation. The film locates legitimate authority not in rank, national sovereignty or force but in the ability to understand and be understood — expertise joined to empathy. Weber commands and Halpern invokes national security, but the film validates the civilian linguist who defies both; legitimacy is further vested in a collective 'non-zero-sum' sharing among all twelve nations, and ultimately in a foreknowledge freely chosen rather than imposed.
skeleton.opening_power: Militaries and intelligence services of twelve nations — in the US, Colonel Weber and CIA Agent Halpern, operating under presidential emergency powers, curfew and radio silence; the heptapods hold the unilateral power of arrival and of opening or closing their door.
skeleton.closing_power: Louise Banks, individually — she takes Halpern's phone, calls Shang, and 'change[s] someone's mind' against direct orders and gun barrels; and thereafter a unified international scientific community sharing all twelve pieces. Military command formally persists but is shown as having been overridden and then superseded by 'this unification.' In the personal frame, Louise holds power over her own life's shape.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Global peace and ordinary life: the war footing is stood down, the blackout ends, the ships depart, and the world returns to functioning without invasion or retaliation.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Linear time as the frame of human experience ('I don't believe in beginnings and endings'), and with it the zero-sum logic of national secrecy, competitive translation and chain-of-command obedience. Louise's grief is permanently re-signified from loss suffered to loss chosen.
skeleton.antagonist: No single antagonist: militarised fear itself, distributed across General Shang's ultimatum, Agent Halpern's insistence on secrecy, the talk-radio agitation, and the rogue soldiers who plant the bomb.
skeleton.antagonist_origin: The soldiers 'have been watching too much TV' and act from panic amid looting, a doomsday cult and a collapsing market; Shang's hostility is retroactively humanised by the disclosure that he is a widower whose wife's dying words can reach him.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Isolation and a defensive relation to time — a woman living alone inside a remembered ending, telling her mother 'I'm about the same,' joking 'I guess that's why I'm single,' and initially reading her visions as intrusions to be hidden ('I don't think that that makes me unfit to do this job').
skeleton.protagonist_change: She TAKES UP what is handed to her: the language explicitly called 'a gift,' and with it foreknowledge of a marriage that will fail and a child who will die, which she accepts rather than avoids — 'Despite knowing the journey and where it leads, I embrace it.' She also puts down obedience to the chain of command, but the film's emphasis is on the acceptance of a burden offered, not the shedding of one imposed.
skeleton.final_image: Louise and Ian embracing in a lit apartment while Louise's narration folds the whole life into the moment: 'I forgot how good it felt to be held by you.' — 'You wanna make a baby?' The last scene asserts that a life whose grief is fully known is still worth choosing, and that the choice, not the outcome, is where meaning sits.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: Yes. Yeah.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The narration is unironic and confessional throughout ('I embrace it. And I welcome every moment of it'), the ending rewards exactly the values the protagonist argues for (openness, trade, 'non-zero-sum game'), and reception describes it as 'introspective, philosophical', 'transcendent', 'genuinely affecting emotion' — no reviewer quoted reads it as satire; the sole hostile notice calls it 'pretentious poopery', a charge of excess sincerity, not irony.
skeleton.source_text: An adaptation — the evidence records an Academy Award nomination for Best Adapted Screenplay — but the supplied evidence never names the source work.

films.title: Hacksaw Ridge
films.description: A man enters a brutal institution determined to serve others without abandoning the principle that defines him.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Individual religious conviction — the divine commandment "Thou shalt not kill" — validated by constitutional/statutory law and finally by demonstrated competence under fire; military command is legitimate but must bend to protected conscience. The film treats the tribunal's ruling ("his rights as a conscientious objector are protected by an Act of Congress") and Doss's battlefield results as jointly settling the question.
skeleton.opening_power: The U.S. Army command hierarchy (Sergeant Howell, Captain Glover, Colonel Sangston, the court-martial) over the enlisted men; in the domestic prologue, Tom Doss's violent paternal authority over the household.
skeleton.closing_power: The same command hierarchy — Glover still commands, the ridge is taken, victory is achieved — but it now defers to Doss's conscience, delaying the assault until his Sabbath prayer ends; Doss himself holds moral authority and is decorated by the state (Medal of Honor from Truman).
skeleton.what_is_restored: The chain of command and the unit's cohesion; Doss's honor and standing among the men who beat and mocked him; the marriage and the promised return home; American victory on the objective.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: The premise that a soldier must bear arms to serve — the unit's and the Army's contempt for pacifism is dismantled from inside, and the men who tried to expel Doss end by refusing to attack without him.
skeleton.antagonist: The coercive apparatus that tries to break Doss's conviction — Sergeant Howell and Captain Glover, backed by the court-martial — with the Japanese army as the impersonal external enemy and Tom Doss's drunken violence as the originating antagonist.
skeleton.antagonist_origin: Tom Doss's brutality is explained by WWI trauma and grief for dead friends ("It's like I died with you"; "I wish you knew him like I did, before the war"), while Howell and Glover's persecution is framed as duty to the lives of the men ("It's about the lives of every man in here").
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Self-doubt about whether his refusal is faith or vanity — the accusation, voiced by Dorothy, that it is "just pride. Pride and stubbornness" — and the temptation to compromise (plead guilty, touch the rifle once) to secure marriage, freedom and belonging.
skeleton.protagonist_change: He does not put anything down; he TAKES UP the conviction he already held and makes it public and costly, refusing every offered exit ("I don't know how I'm going to live with myself if I don't stay true to what I believe"), and then takes up the vocation and honors handed to him — medic's authority, Glover's apology, the men's trust, the Medal of Honor.
skeleton.final_image: Archival footage of the real Desmond Doss receiving the Medal of Honor and, in interview shortly before his death, recounting washing the blood from a wounded man's eyes — asserting that the conviction the whole film tested was literally true, historically vindicated, and repaid by one man's smile.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: And if I hadn't got anything more out of the war than that smile he gave me, I'd have been well repaid.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The ending validates Doss without irony: the officers who persecuted him apologise, the assault is held for his prayers, the state decorates him, and the film cuts to the real man's testimony. Reception confirms the register — the critical consensus calls it "a gripping wartime tribute to faith, valor, and the courage of remaining true to one's convictions," and it won a "Faith & Freedom Award." The only dissenting notes (Seitz's "a movie at war with itself," the charge that the Japanese are drawn as "crazed and animalistic") describe an unexamined tension, not an intended critique.
skeleton.source_text: The wartime life of Desmond T. Doss (the closing archival interview and Medal of Honor footage are presented as the film's source and warrant).

films.title: Joker
films.description: An isolated man searches for dignity in a city that repeatedly treats suffering as someone else’s problem.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: The film locates legitimate authority nowhere stable: inherited wealth and civic paternalism (Thomas Wayne, 'I'm their only hope') are shown as contemptuous and self-serving, institutional care (social services, Arkham, police) as underfunded and indifferent, and the crowd's insurrectionary force as the only power that actually responds — legitimacy is treated as belonging to whoever is seen and heard, and the film grants that recognition to the abandoned rather than to the propertied.
skeleton.opening_power: Gotham's monied and institutional elite — billionaire mayoral candidate Thomas Wayne, Mayor Stokes, the police, employers like Hoyt and Wayne Investments, and media figures like Murray Franklin who set what counts as funny and who counts at all; Arthur is at the bottom, dependent on a city social-services caseworker for medication.
skeleton.closing_power: No governing authority holds the city: Wayne and Murray are dead, the police are overwhelmed, riots are general, and the masked crowd owns the streets and elevates Arthur atop a wrecked police car; in the last scene, however, Arthur himself is again institutionally confined at Arkham with an orderly chasing him — power over him restored to the asylum even as civic order is not restored.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Only Arthur's confinement — he ends institutionalized at Arkham, as his mother was and as he had been before ('I think I felt better when I was locked up in the hospital'). The social order itself is not restored.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: The civic hierarchy: the Wayne family's untouchability (Thomas and Martha murdered in the alley), the talk-show establishment's authority to define who is a joke (Murray shot on air), the police's control of the streets, and Arthur's own self-image as a man who must 'put on a happy face' — he discards the diagnosis of his laugh as illness ('That's the real me').
skeleton.antagonist: A composite social order embodied in Thomas Wayne and Murray Franklin — the wealthy patron who calls the poor 'clowns' and the host who broadcasts Arthur's humiliation for laughs.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Arthur's compulsive deference and manufactured cheer — his belief in the mother's instruction to 'smile and put on a happy face,' his need to be loved by Murray and claimed by Wayne, and his acceptance of the story others tell about him (that his laugh is a condition, that he was put here to spread joy).
skeleton.protagonist_change: He puts down the imposed persona rather than taking up any office or inheritance: he stops the medication, rejects the name 'Happy' and the fiction of a father, renames himself Joker on live television, and reclassifies his life from tragedy to comedy — 'I used to think that my life was a tragedy... But now I realize it's a fucking comedy.' What replaces the flaw is not virtue but self-authorship through violence.
skeleton.final_image: Arthur in a white Arkham room laughing at a joke he refuses to explain to his therapist, then walking away down a corridor leaving bloodied footprints while an orderly chases him — asserting that the making of him is complete, unrepentant and beyond the reach of the institution's understanding.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: You wouldn't get it.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The telling is locked to Arthur's perspective — fantasy sequences, the dance-as-liberation, the crowd's adulation scored to triumph — and the ending rewards his transformation with recognition rather than refutation. Reception evidence names the ambivalence outright rather than resolving it into irony: Chauncey Robinson says it 'walks a fine line between exploration and validation'; Alison Willmore calls the politics 'impossible' and 'deliberately contradictory'; Richard Lawson finds it 'too sympathetic towards white men who commit heinous crimes.' Countervailing readings call it a 'cautionary tale' and 'a fairly straightforward condemnation of American austerity,' and Phillips insists it is 'certainly not a political film.' The film critiques the order that produces Arthur but does not distance itself from Arthur's frame, so this is not the depict-without-endorsing case.
skeleton.source_text: DC Comics Batman mythology (the Joker; Thomas, Martha and Bruce Wayne; Arkham; Alfred Pennyworth); reception also names Taxi Driver and The King of Comedy as models.
skeleton.inverts_source_how: It centres the villain and grants him the interiority normally reserved for Batman, making the Waynes' murder the crowd's judgement rather than an atrocity that founds a hero; Thomas Wayne, ordinarily a benevolent patriarch, is rendered a contemptuous plutocrat, and Bruce is a bystander to Arthur's story rather than its subject.

punished: the three Wayne Investments men on the subway
forgiven: Gary, spared for having been the only one kind to Arthur

films.title: Parasite
films.description: Two families from sharply different circumstances become entangled in a fragile arrangement shaped by need and status.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: Money and property. The film shows authority flowing entirely from wealth — who owns the house commands everyone in it — and treats that as an arbitrary, unearned fact rather than a moral entitlement: 'Not "rich, but still nice." "Nice because she's rich."' and 'Money is an iron. Those creases all get smoothed out.' No competing legitimacy (law, merit, consent) is offered as sound; even the con and the police resolution are shown as products of the same economic sorting.
skeleton.opening_power: The Park family, who own the architect-designed hillside house and hire, fire and dismiss at whim; the Kim family are jobless, in a semi-basement, stealing wi-fi and folding pizza boxes for a docked wage.
skeleton.closing_power: A new wealthy family (German) owns the same house; Ki-taek is hidden in its bunker, dependent on their leavings; Ki-woo and Chung-sook are back in a semi-basement flat. The structure is unchanged, only its occupants swapped.
skeleton.what_is_restored: The vertical order itself: a rich family above ground, a servant class attending them, and a man living unseen in the cellar. The house is sold and refilled, the murders are officially unexplained ('the homeless man who sparked the rampage... police are struggling to even establish a clear motive'), and the poor return to the basement level they started from.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Nothing structural. Only lives are destroyed: Ki-jung is dead, Mr Park is dead, Moon-gwang and Geun-sae are dead, Ki-taek is a permanent fugitive underground, Ki-woo brain-damaged and on probation. The deference Ki-taek performed for Mr Park is broken in a single irreversible act, but it changes no arrangement.
skeleton.antagonist: The class arrangement itself, embodied in Mr Park's fastidious contempt ('that smell crosses the line'); proximately Geun-sae and Moon-gwang, rival poor who threaten exposure.
skeleton.antagonist_origin: Geun-sae's Taiwanese castella shop went bust, he borrowed from loan sharks who still threaten to stab him, and he has lived four years in the bunker fed secretly by his wife — the same failed-business path Ki-taek himself walked.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: The Kims' belief that cunning can carry them across the line — forged documents, borrowed names, the fantasy of 'fitting in' — paired with Ki-taek's fatalism ('You know what kind of plan never fails? No plan at all') and his swallowed humiliation at being smelled and ordered about.
skeleton.protagonist_change: Ki-taek stops absorbing contempt and kills Mr Park, then puts himself down into the bunker — he puts down servitude and takes up literal imprisonment. Ki-woo ends by TAKING UP something he hands himself: 'today I made a plan. A fundamental plan. I'm going to earn money... When I have money, I'll buy that house.' The film immediately cuts back to the semi-basement, marking the vow as inherited delusion rather than transformation.
skeleton.final_image: A fantasy of Ki-woo buying the house and his father walking up out of the cellar into sunlight, which dissolves back to Ki-woo alone in the semi-basement flat — the ascent asserted only as wish, the basement asserted as fact.
skeleton.final_spoken_line: So long.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The film stages the con and the Parks' comfort at length while systematically undercutting both: the Kims' articulated theory of wealth ('Nice because she's rich'), Mr Park's revulsion at the smell of subway riders spoken from a sofa he thinks is private, and the closing dissolve that exposes the upward plan as fantasy. Reception names the anger outright — 'he is unmistakably, roaringly furious, and it registers because the target is so deserving' — and 'a tick fat with the bitter blood of class rage'; critics read it as social commentary and class consciousness, not as a caper endorsing either family.

the Kim family collectively (their private deliberations, jokes, shame)
punished: Ki-woo (bludgeoned, brain surgery, convicted of fraud, probation)
forgiven: Ki-taek, insofar as his son answers the letter rather than condemning it ('Take care until then')

films.title: Wicked
films.description: Two unlikely friends navigate a public story that turns difference into danger and loyalty into a costly choice.

skeleton.legitimacy_source: The film locates legitimate authority in truth-telling conscience and self-determination rather than in office or acclamation; the ruling Wizard is explicitly a fraud with no real power, and the only genuine magic belongs to the outcast who reads the Grimmerie. Popular consent is shown to be manufactured (Morrible 'denounces her to all of Oz'), so mass approval is not treated as legitimating.
skeleton.opening_power: The Wizard of Oz rules the Land of Oz, 'famed for his power to grant wishes,' administered through Madame Morrible and institutions like Shiz University; Glinda the Good is the publicly celebrated figure in the frame narrative.
skeleton.closing_power: Unchanged at the top: the Wizard and Morrible still rule Oz and have successfully branded Elphaba wicked; Glinda remains inside the regime by choice; Elphaba holds only personal power — the Grimmerie and flight — as a fugitive outside the order. The frame narrative confirms the regime outlasts her.
skeleton.what_is_restored: Nothing is restored; the frame's opening celebration of the Witch's death shows the official order intact and triumphant.
skeleton.what_is_overturned: Elphaba's own belief in the Wizard's benevolence, and her wish to be accepted by the order — she permanently abandons both, along with her ambition to serve; the friendship's naivety is ended by the farewell.
skeleton.antagonist: The Wizard, with Madame Morrible as his instrument and Oz's institutional persecution of the Animals
skeleton.antagonist_origin: The Wizard is revealed to be 'an ordinary man,' a fraud 'unable to read the Grimmerie and lacking real magic of his own,' whose authority depends on manufacturing spectacle and enemies; the plot also implies he is the traveling salesman who fathered Elphaba.
skeleton.protagonist_flaw: Elphaba's shame at being marked and rejected, and her credulous faith that the authority above her is good and will 'set it right' if only she is useful enough to it
skeleton.protagonist_change: She PUTS DOWN the imposed hope of approval — refusing to apologize, rejecting the Wizard's patronage and the name Oz gives her — and in the same motion TAKES UP the stolen Grimmerie and her own unlicensed power, choosing exile and flight over sanctioned belonging.
skeleton.final_image: Elphaba, having levitated a broom, flies west alone, leaving Glinda behind amid a mass evacuation from Shiz — asserting that integrity here means departure and solitude, not victory, and that the wicked label is a lie the state has successfully told.
skeleton.endorsement_evidence: The frame narrative is told by Glinda to a crowd celebrating the Witch's death and explaining 'why wickedness happens' — an account the body of the film systematically contradicts, so the official version is depicted and disowned. Reception confirms the film is read as sincerely anti-authoritarian rather than endorsing Oz's order: critics name 'the movie's heavier themes of authoritarianism' and 'Authoritarianism and broad comedy make strange and uneasy bedfellows.' The tone toward Elphaba herself is sincere, not ironic ('effervescence and sincerity').
skeleton.source_text: The Wizard of Oz / the Land of Oz stories, via the stage musical Wicked (the evidence calls it 'this prequel to The Wizard of Oz' and 'the stage musical')
skeleton.inverts_source_how: The Wicked Witch of the West is recast as the moral protagonist and the Wizard as a fraudulent oppressor; 'wickedness' is shown to be a label manufactured by the state to discredit a whistleblower, and Glinda the Good is complicit rather than purely virtuous.
